extracted.intended_audience: early-18th-century literate public; coffeehouse readers and readers of The Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: A short, periodical essay (Spectator-style) giving moral and social commentary on duelling, manners, character types (toasts, rakes, smart fellows), and practical advice about counsel and choice of associates. Normative and satirical guidance aimed at urban readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism of the diamond and the glass for a toast
rubrics_metrics.description: The hieroglyphic of the diamond is to show her, that her value is imaginary; and that of the glass to acquaint her, that her condition is frail, and depends on the hand which holds her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This design admonishes the toast neither to overrate nor depreciate her charms; whether a toast is honoured ('eaten') or rejected ('left as an offal') depends on the humour and taste of the company. (Used as social advice about self-regard and awareness of public opinion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits distinguishing types of celebrated beauties (Gatty vs Frontlet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between two dominant toast-types: Gatty (an agreeable beauty) and Frontlet (an awful/solemn beauty). Gatty 'for ever smiles upon you'; Frontlet 'disdains to see you smile.' 'Gatty's love is a shining quick flame; Frontlet's a slow wasting fire.' Gatty likes the man that diverts her; Frontlet him who adores her.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their different manners determine who admires them (wits & coxcombs vs politicians & pretenders). The 'reign' of such a beauty should be judged by duration: convivial, easy charms endure (Gatty) while solemn, austere beauty (Frontlet) has limited appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and practical absurdity of 'giving a man satisfaction' (duelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: By this means it is called, 'giving a man satisfaction,' to urge your offence against him with your sword; illustrated by a pointed rephrasing of a typical challenge to show its internal contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'satisfaction' as used in challenges is shown to be incoherent (the insult is met by a demand to be shot through the head), exposing duels as a senseless ritual rather than a rational remedy for insult. Use this to critique the custom and to show why duels defend folly rather than honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to attack the custom of duelling effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat this custom with humour and raillery to get an audience, before you come to pronounce sentence upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use satire, ridicule, and practical demonstration (e.g., public lists of those 'qualified' to duel) to create aversion to the practice. A humorous, public exposure of the characters who fight will persuade the audience more than solemn moralising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rules for giving advice (how to counsel others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people will ask counsel of you, when they have already acted... The sure way is to tell him, that is certainly to be chosen. Then you are to be very clear and positive; leave no handle for scruple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many seekers want confirmation of what they already intend; to influence them you may either mirror their inclination or, when stakes require honesty, be candid. If aiming to satisfy the petitioner rather than change him, give clear, decisive counsel without ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for selecting a guardian/master for a young man (Paulo vs Avaro)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paulo's habitation 'has at once the air of a nobleman and a merchant. You see the servants act with affection to their master; the master meets you with an open countenance, full of benevolence and integrity: your business is despatched with that confidence and welcome which always accompanies honest minds: his table is the image of plenty and generosity, supported by justice and frugality.' Avaro appears suspicious, mean, 'lived like a beggar,' and profits at others' expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a guardian who improves those around him (benefits customers, treats servants well, shows openness and integrity) rather than one who accumulates wealth by harming others or by being meanly suspicious. The mentor's moral economy shapes the youth's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social markers of classes of fops: 'pretty fellows' and 'smart fellows'
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions and trappings used to identify pretenders: some style-signs include calling each other Betty/Nelly, accosting with effeminate airs, having signs and tokens, hanging a cane on a button, wearing red-heeled shoes, never paying at the playhouse, and other ostentatious or affected behaviours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These outward signs are satirically enumerated as criteria for social classification: adopt them to lampoon or to exclude such pretensions. The author assigns formal exclusion/admission (enrolling) based on these affectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation and moral assessment of the 'rake'
rubrics_metrics.description: A Rake is a man always to be pitied; his faults proceed not from choice or inclination, but from strong passions and appetites... he errs and repents, and repents and errs on. He cannot use his own reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the rake with pity rather than scorn: his vicious repetition stems from weakness of self-control, not deliberate malice. This distinction informs how society should judge and attempt to reform him.
